entries.title: FBI Probes Hackers' Claim of Stealing Employee Data, Compromising Jobs Website
entries.summary: The FBI jobs portal remained offline after the group claimed to hack the site.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

The FBI said Wednesday that it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claims that it had stolen “very sensitive data” belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website.

“The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information," the FBI said in a statement. It said that while the “point of breach” was undetermined, "we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”

The jobs website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline as of Wednesday afternoon.

A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack.

“We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job,” said the ShinyHunters message, which was directed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Brett Leatherman, the assistant director in charge of the bureau's cyber division.

The claims could not immediately be verified. An email to an address associated with ShinyHunters was not immediately returned.

The hackers are seeking retribution over an FBI advisory

Miriam Wugmeister, a lawyer specializing in data, privacy and cybercrime who tracks hacking outfits like ShinyHunters, said that based on the group's past practices, there was reason to believe the hackers' claims, “so I think it’s likely that they were able to compromise this website and they got some data.”

She said that though the data that appeared to be compromised was the type of personal information that is routinely accessed during a breach, the hack nonetheless had alarming national security implications given that it could expose agents and their families to extortion, swatting and other harassment and because the identities of spouses were also said to have been obtained.

“Even if the agents and the analysts and the employees are sophisticated, you worry about their families too,” she said.

In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it said were false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”

That advisory characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was “offended” by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. It did not say what would happen if the FBI did not do so within a week.

“This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated,” the hacking group's message said.

ShinyHunters has a reputation for “causing trouble and being disruptive,” Wugmeister said, as evidenced by the group’s involvement in a hack last spring of Canvas, an online system used by thousands of schools and universities. The breach created chaos as students tried to study for finals and prompted the FBI’s advisory that ShinyHunters is now objecting to.

There have been other cyber incidents concerning the FBI

The hack was first reported by 404 Media, an online technology publication that said a representative of ShinyHunters shared what appeared to be a sample of personal data of 5,000 FBI employees, including addresses, phone numbers and some information on spouses.

The publication said the ShinyHunters representative said the group carried out the hack through an apparent vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft software, commonly used by companies and government agencies for large-scale data processing and human resources purposes. The FBI said in its statement that it had not determined whether the “point of breach” involved a “third-party or the FBI’s enterprise.”

The FBI, the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, has been a common target for hackers.

In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appeared to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.

The FBI described the compromised information as “historical in nature” and said it involved "no government information.”

entries.title: Court Filing Says Kennedy Center Hazards Prompted Closing, Not Trump’s Threats
entries.summary: The center’s executive director said the center could reopen once safety issues are addressed.
entries.content:
Kennedy Center officials said in a court filing Wednesday that the shuttered building could reopen once major safety hazards detailed in a new report are fixed — even as President Donald Trump has cast the center’s future on whether he gets his name engraved on the landmark.

The status report filed by the Justice Department in federal court offers a narrower explanation for the shutdown than Trump’s warning that the center could end up “ripped down” if he is not recognized on the building.

A sworn declaration from Executive Director Matt Floca details several “hazard and life-safety concerns,” including collapsing ceiling panels, water-infiltrating electrical transformers and concerns about unsafe theater equipment, but contains no finding that the center needs to be demolished.

The center’s Trump-appointed board voted last week to close the venue during the $250 million renovations. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) is fighting the closure in her role as an ex officio board member, arguing that the shutdown violates an existing court order from Judge Christopher R. Cooper and could be a pretext for something permanent.

Floca said he extended the temporary closure for another week “to protect employees, patrons, artists, contractors, and other members of the public while the Center evaluated documented falling-object hazards and other infrastructure conditions and determined what measures would be required for safe occupancy and emergency egress,” according to the report.

The filing included new details about the building’s condition, centering around the severe storms that pummeled D.C. earlier this month, in which “a large section of ceiling plaster weighing approximately 150 pounds fell from approximately 60 feet to the floor in a public thoroughfare.”

Water apparently also made its way into an electrical transformer vault, according to a Tuesday inspection by WB Engineers+Consultants. The contractor also discovered concrete fragments and other debris on the equipment, according to the court filing.

Staff also flagged problems with opera house lighting supports and counterweight rigging systems.

Floca said that the emergency shutdown is separate from the board’s longer-term closure plan. Wednesday’s filing says interim safeguards would not resolve the underlying deterioration or determine the scope or duration of a larger renovation.

After the center’s board approved the closure, Trump asserted that renovations would stay off the table altogether unless he received a favorable court decision.

“The Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on Truth Social.

The court filing provides no firm reopening date.

Beatty’s attorneys did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s requests for comment.

entries.title: Republicans Break With Trump After Immigration Crackdowns Hit Home
entries.summary: Republicans are signaling they see it as a vulnerability in some of the country’s most competitive races.
entries.content:
Several Republican candidates in competitive races are criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, signaling that they see it as a vulnerability in a political landscape that seems poised to favor Democrats.

The immigration agenda, a hallmark of President Donald Trump’s campaigns, has led to major deportation operations across the country — including in some of the states where Republicans are actively breaking with him on the issue.

Just this week, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican running for Congress in the state’s competitive 2nd Congressional District, told reporters that ICE should prioritize “people in the gangs and criminals first” while sharing that his son’s father-in-law is currently facing deportation despite holding a work permit.

“He came from a country that's not to the liking of certain people in Washington,” LePage said at a press conference in Augusta, Maine, on Monday, but didn’t say more about the man. “That’s not right.”

LePage’s campaign did not respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment. The state where LePage is running was the site of an immigration enforcement operation in January. In July, federal immigration agents shot a man in Biddeford, Maine, and prompted Republican Sen. Susan Collins to call on Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to cease all non-essential traffic stops in the state. The administration did, until Trump reversed the decision.

Several issues are causing rifts between the White House and Republican candidates, particularly those in tough races. Earlier this week, for example, two Republicans — Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson and Michigan senate candidate Mike Rogers — called for a swift end to the president’s war in Iran.

Immigration has been a similar lightning rod, and Democrats are on the offensive over it. They see the administration’s policies on immigration as an issue that will move voters towards their party come November.

The Trump administration has implemented a large-scale mass deportation campaign that has involved sweeping enforcement with a historic amount of funding going toward the Department of Homeland Security, and more than 610,000 people across the country detained since the president’s inauguration last January, according to The Marshall Project.

The Trump administration has increasingly restricted pathways of legal immigration as well, resulting in many people losing their legal status and protections. The aggressive immigration tactics appear to be posing a problem for candidates as the midterms inch closer.

The Republican who has perhaps been the most direct in criticizing the president’s immigration agenda is from Florida. Rep. María Elvira Salazar released an ad last week criticizing Trump’s immigration policies.

Salazar, who is also running in a competitive district, warned Trump that “some of your immigration enforcements have gone too far.” “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” the lawmaker, who represents a heavily Latino and immigrant district, continued.

Texas Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is rated “lean Republican” by Cook Political Report, put out an ad earlier this month featuring the story of a DACA recipient who was detained by ICE. The ad suggests that De La Cruz helped release the man from detention.

De La Cruz’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Her state has also seen high-profile consequences of Trump’s immigration agenda play out, including ICE officers shooting a man in Austin over the weekend. The man’s lawyer told CNN he is facing partial paralysis. That incident happened just two months after officers fatally shot a man in Houston.

The White House did not comment on the Republicans distancing themselves from Trump.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said he understood Salazar’s position, but that he just doesn’t “happen to be there.”

“She’s got a little bit soft on the border,” Trump, who has endorsed Salazar’s reelection bid, said. “I understand that.”

While those three candidates mark recent breaks in the party, at least one other vulnerable Republican has been holding the immigration aspect of the Trump agenda at arm’s length for longer.

New York Rep. Mike Lawler, who is running in one of the most competitive districts in the nation and who like Salazar and De La Cruz voted for last summer’s spending bill that gave record-level funding to DHS, has also praised the president’s high number of deportations. But he has called for DHS to reassess its tactics.

“Americans are increasingly concerned about the Department of Homeland Security’s enforcement operations,” Lawler wrote in an op-ed published in The New York Times following fatal shootings by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis. His campaign referred The Sun to the op-ed.

In an ad that first aired last week, Lawler touted his support for the Dignity Act — a bill co-sponsored by Salazar that would create steps through which long-term undocumented immigrants would be able to apply for legal status.

“I’m working hard on the Dignity Act, so that everyone can reach the American Dream,” Lawler said in Spanish in the ad.

entries.title: How Progressive Powerhouses Put Their Endorsements to Work
entries.summary: The high-profile support can drive millions to candidates, but the timing makes a difference according to The Washington Sun’s analysis.
entries.content:
The older crowd may be on the outs for progressive Democrats, but if younger candidates want a campaign boost, the left wing’s old guard is where to turn first, a Washington Sun analysis of high-profile progressive endorsers finds.

It also found differing strategies in how the leading figures on the left decide when to formally bless aspirants to the U.S. House and Senate.

The analysis, which crunched data on endorsements from a number of leading figures on the left and subsequent donations from the endorsers’ networks in the current election cycle, found that through July 31 donors in Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders’ network contributed the most, followed by that of California Rep. Ro Khanna.

The Sanders imprimatur spurred his backers to dole out $9.1 million to 21 chosen candidates, for an average of more than $433,000, though the largest amount, $3.1 million went to the now-defunct Senate campaign of Maine’s Graham Platner. Khanna backed 15 congressional hopefuls, enticing his network to hand out an average of $227,000 to each campaign for a total of $3.4 million.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/jyU5U/1/Among high-profile Democrats like Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York) and Ilhan Omar (Michigan), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Massachusetts), Warren has generated the most endorsements and donations, picking 11 congressional candidates and helping generate nearly $2.7 million, an average of more than $242,000 per candidate.

Ocasio-Cortez and Omar have been more conservative in naming favorites. Before the analysis’ July 31 cut off, the New York representative anointed seven candidates, who received $1.8 million from her network for an average of over $257,000. Omar threw her support behind nine candidates who landed nearly $1.6 million, or just under $174,000 a piece.

The data also reveal differing strategies, with Sanders and Khanna taking a riskier endorse-often and endorse-early approach. Sanders’ backing came a median of 103 days before his choices’ primaries. Khanna’s median is 96. Warren’s median endorsement date is also a relatively long 82 days ahead of time.

In the case of Khanna, who harbors national ambitions but isn’t as well-known, the early aid can be helpful in raising his profile and building gratitude with up and coming progressives. He’s also backed numerous non-federal candidates. In Sanders’ case, it marks a shift, said Julian Mulvey, one of the architects of Sanders’ first presidential campaign.

He told The Washington Sun it once “took a long time” for candidates to earn the Vermont senator’s support, but “that’s changed” with this cycle’s slate of endorsements. He praised Sanders and Khanna for their aggressive strategies, which helped raise resources and the profiles of left-leaning candidates who have won primaries.

Sanders supporters like Mulvey acknowledged the risk of a shoot-fast-and-early endorsement strategy. Platner is the prime example, having soared to prominence with help from the millions Sanders’ donors forked over only to drop his bid in July amid allegations of sexual assault. Sanders endorsed Platner 283 days before his primary victory in June, and stood by the oysterman through numerous earlier flare ups before calling for Platner to quit after assault allegations became public.

Neither Ocasio-Cortez nor Omar ever endorsed Platner.

They wait until late, functioning more like closers in the final innings of primaries. Omar has endorsed candidates less than a month before their primaries — a median of 29 days. For Ocasio-Cortez, it’s just 20 days before the election.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/KIZxv/1/While the slower endorsements could be seen as a sort of Johnny-come-lately caution, it can also reflect the extraordinary — and often hostile — attention directed at the pair, especially at Ocasio-Cortez.

“I don’t think anyone can quite appreciate the astonishing level of scrutiny that falls on her, it is like no one else in the party,” Mulvey said about Ocasio-Cortez. “I give her a tremendous amount of leeway to figure this out, because no one else has to face that level or scrutiny. I don’t blame her at all for being very careful, very judicious.”

The later endorsements also have the effect of delivering a more concentrated stream of cash that comes in over a compressed time frame, perhaps when it’s needed most.

For instance, Sanders backed the Senate campaign of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan a full 474 days before the primary, and Khanna followed with an endorsement just a week later. Sanders supporters contributed nearly $2.1 million to El-Sayed after the endorsement, and Khanna’s network added just shy of $1 million.

Ocasio-Cortez endorsed El-Sayed just 33 days before his primary, and Omar threw her support behind the Michigan progressive 22 days before the election as the race was tightening. In the time after the endorsements, Ocasio-Cortez donors gave El-Sayed over $940,000 and Omar’s network contributed almost $735,000.

Another progressive strategist said the endorsements from Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and other leaders in the movement, no matter when they come through, are needed to capitalize on an environment that is “very amenable to progressive challengers.”

“Organizing is great, but even that requires money,” the strategist said. “Because progressive voters are extremely invested, a little money goes a lot further with them.”

The Sun determined the impacts of the endorsers by analyzing federal campaign finance records to identify donors who contributed to the progressive congressional leaders over several election cycles, then calculating how much those donors contributed in the 2026 midterm cycle to the campaigns that each lawmaker endorsed. Donors were matched using normalized names and ZIP codes. The analysis also examined the timing of endorsements, including how far ahead of an election they were made and when a leader’s donors began giving to endorsed candidates. The analysis supplemented Federal Election Commission data with ActBlue earmarked contribution data to capture small-dollar donations that do not always appear individually in a candidate’s FEC filings.
entries.author: Stephen Neukam

entries.title: Trump’s Domestic Woes Are Growing. He’ll Throw Xi a Lavish Visit Anyway.
entries.summary: Crucial geopolitical negotiations — and lavish White House events — come as Trump navigates a sharp downturn in his second term.
entries.content:
When President Donald Trump welcomes President Xi Jinping of China to the White House on Thursday, it will be at a low point in his second term. Republicans are rebelling on issues that are personal to the president: an expensive gift to his son, a media ban, mass deportations, the Iran war — even Xi's visit. Polls and surveys show him with his lowest approval rating. Trump even seems to have given up on Republicans maintaining control of Congress in November’s midterms.

Meanwhile, Xi arrives preparing to lay the groundwork for his next five-year term, believing he’s visiting a nation in decline and granting Trump a visit the president has sought since before his second inauguration.

“There's a really unfortunate split screen here for the United States,” said Jonathan Czin, the director for China on the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden.

But as the fractions deepen within the Republican Party, Trump has turned his attention to reciprocating the reception he received in China earlier this year.

Although Trump greeted Xi when the Chinese president arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday — the first time since 1962 a president has personally welcomed a foreign leader at JBA — the summit truly kicks off Thursday with a lavish and meticulously planned day of events at the White House.

It's expected to be a continuation of Wednesday’s pageantry, when Xi stepped off his plane and onto a red carpet with a dozen fighter jets to his right, an artillery salute to his left and two B-1 bombers shrieking low overhead. But while some are dismayed by the extravagance, current and former U.S. officials and China policy experts say it is key to the success of the first Chinese state visit to Washington in 11 years.

Daniel R. Russel, who served as the assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during Xi’s 2015 state visit, told The Washington Sun the opulence is the cost of doing business with the Chinese, who he said are reluctant to travel to the U.S. without the prestige a state visit brings. It’s a projection of China’s superpower status, Russel added, even as it sees a distinctive change in its relationship with the U.S.

“The relationship is very different. A lot of it boils down to the shift in relative strength and leverage between Beijing and Washington,” Russel said. “The Chinese leadership is feeling very strong right now compared to the U.S., that they’ve got a considerable amount of leverage, a reasonable analysis of Trump and how to manipulate him.”

In May, a Chinese official told The Sun that the country spent weeks preparing for Trump’s visit to Beijing, a visit punctuated by pomp and circumstance at every event and interaction. Trump has sought to return the favor.

Last week on the White House grounds, reporters could see military rehearsals in anticipation of Xi’s arrival. The administration planned a multilayered welcome for Xi, with a ceremony that will move from the South Lawn to the state floor and the Rose Garden. A flyover by stealth aircraft will cap a military parade of 479 personnel for Xi and his wife, Madam Peng Liyuan. The day is scheduled to end with a state dinner curated by first lady Melania Trump and featuring some of America’s most powerful business leaders.

Melania Trump told Fox News on Wednesday that there were “a lot of details” to plan for a state dinner.

“There is protocol that you need to follow,” she said, adding she was involved in every detail.

An Obama-era official involved in planning the 2015 state dinner, Xi’s last in the U.S., said a dinner for the Chinese president brought heightened pressure compared with other foreign dignitaries.

“We had to be very precise about everything,” the Obama official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to speak freely. “And I mean that's every state dinner, but China, there is a history of a contentious relationship that we had to consider and make sure everything was to a T.”

Barack Obama, Xi Jinping 790376218435 (4004x2848, AR: 1.41)
Fearing they might accidentally insult the Chinese, the official said, “our main [goal] was to be so detailed … making sure that we didn't offend or do anything that would mess up any conversations or be a talking point later on.”

Some people aren’t pleased that Xi is here at all. Protesters forced the military to close an access point at JBA during Xi’s arrival. Others marched downtown Wednesday night chanting, “End the CCP!” And Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) denounced the visit during a floor speech on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio brushed off concerns about the displays. When asked by The Sun to respond to Wicker’s comments, Rubio defended the lavishness of Xi’s reception, saying that the relationship between the two nations would “define the 21st century.”

“The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It's outrageous,” Rubio said. “So we have, I think, an obligation to be able to interact and speak at the highest levels. And I think that's what this visit reflects, is the president's belief that no matter what our disagreements and differences may be with the Chinese government, this is not some small country.”
entries.author: Jasmine Wright, Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Security Concerns Spur D.C. to Consider Privacy Protections for Judges
entries.summary: One federal judge is said to have received dozens of unsolicited pizza deliveries.
entries.content:
The D.C. Council is considering giving local and federal judges the ability to request that information about them — including their home address, personal phone numbers and the names of family members — be removed from public and private databases, a step that advocates say is needed to ensure their security in an era of increasing threats to jurists.

The bill, introduced by council Chair Phil Mendelson, would cover Supreme Court justices; federal judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals, U.S. District Court and U.S. Bankruptcy Court; and judges in D.C. Superior Court and the D.C. Court of Appeals. It would prohibit individuals, the government and businesses from disclosing judges’ personal information if a request is made that it not be shared.

The legislation was drafted at the request of Judge Robert Wilkins of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, who reached out to Mendelson in September 2024 to press the matter, indicating that he had been the victim of doxing. He noted that D.C. allows victims of domestic violence to shield their personal information, and asked that judges be offered the same opportunity.

“Unfortunately, there are people who want to use threats to intimidate judges, or even worse, to harm or kill judges as retribution for our rulings. Such actions are not just attacks on the individual judges, they are attacks on our system of justice and the rule of law itself,” Wilkins wrote in testimony submitted to the council ahead of a hearing Wednesday.

Wilkins recounted a number of local cases of judges being threatened or killed, including Maryland Circuit Court Judge Andrew Wilkinson, who was shot and killed in 2023 by a man whose divorce proceedings he was overseeing. The killing spurred legislative action to protect judges’ privacy in Maryland; Mendelson’s bill is modeled after what Maryland lawmakers approved.

Wilkins also cited threats faced by Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and an incident this year at the home of Justice Amy Coney Barrett where someone called 911 and falsely reported gunshots in hopes of provoking a large police response. Wilkins also said one of his own colleagues had been subject to dozens of unsolicited pizza deliveries in D.C.

“Officials with the U.S. Marshals Office tell me that there have been at least 64 recent incidents when a pizza was delivered to the home of one of our D.C. federal judges by a stranger, and many of those deliveries came with a message referencing Judge Esther Salas, a federal judge whose husband and son were shot at the front door of her New Jersey home in 2020, by a disgruntled litigant posing as a delivery man,” he wrote.

An August report from the University of California, Berkeley, and New York University law schools found that while criticism of the courts and individual judicial decisions are part and parcel of a democracy, intensifying political polarization has taken those disagreements to a more troubling level.

“Threats of violence, intimidation, and disinformation directed at judges, and defiance of court orders go beyond healthy criticism and fundamentally threaten judicial independence,” said the report. “Attacks of this nature are not new. But in recent years, the experience of federal judges and data indicate that the frequency and severity of such attacks have escalated significantly.”

Those sorts of attacks and threats can be distinctly present in D.C., Wilkins told Mendelson in his original letter in late 2024 requesting legislative action.

“We handle numerous cases of national interest and which spur heated controversy, including all of the criminal cases from the January 6, 2021 insurrection,” he wrote.

Congress adopted a federal law to better shield judges’ personal information in late 2022, and this summer Barrett and Justice Elena Kagan testified before Congress on the need for more security for judges. Still, Wilkins and other advocates say that state-level action is also necessary.

While the D.C. bill has support, the devil will be in the details. Local supporters of Mendelson’s bill say it will need to simplify the process for judges in D.C. to request that their personal information be removed from public and private databases.

“Suppose a judge buys a home, registers to vote, enrolls her children in public school, applies for a permit to build a fence around her home, and calls 311 to have the remains of her old fence picked up as bulk trash. That judge’s home address is now in the databases of at least six different D.C. agencies,” said Misty Thomas Zaleski of the Council for Court Excellence.

While the majority of the threats have been faced by federal judges, Doug Buchanan, a spokesperson for D.C.’s local courts, said it would similarly provide local judges “some added security barriers between the judiciary and those that they serve.”
